analysis.one_liner: Lets workers redirect part of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 19, 2001 with 7 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Workers born in 1948 or later could elect, irrevocably, to have a share of their Social Security-taxable wages deposited into an individual account instead of flowing only into the trust fund. The account would be invested 60% in broad stock indexes and 40% in government transition bonds, and at retirement the traditional benefit would be reduced by the value of the annuity the account pays. The bill also issues every beneficiary a legally enforceable certificate guaranteeing current-law benefits and cost-of-living adjustments, and orders a study on eventually handing account management to approved private-sector firms.
analysis.who_benefits: Electing workers born in 1948 or later, especially lower earners, who would own a real, inheritable account: the deposit rate is 8% of wages for the lowest earners, sliding to 3% at the wage cap. Account balances above what is needed to replicate current-law benefits could be taken as cash or left to a spouse or children, and every beneficiary would hold a legally enforceable guarantee of current-law benefits with annual inflation adjustments.

how_it_helps.text: Workers born on or after January 1, 1948 could elect to have a percentage of their Social Security-taxable wages deposited into an individual account — 8% for the lowest earners, declining to 3% for those at the wage cap.
Account balances would be invested 60% in broad, board-selected stock indexes and 40% in government Social Security Transition Bonds.

Balances above the amount needed to fund an annuity matching current-law benefits could be taken as a cash distribution, and any remaining balance at death goes to a spouse's account or the worker's beneficiaries.
Every current and future beneficiary would receive a legally enforceable benefit guarantee certificate locking in current-law benefit amounts and annual cost-of-living adjustments.
Retirement annuities drawn from accounts must be indexed to inflation, and married account owners' annuities must include a survivor benefit of two-thirds for the surviving spouse.
General Treasury money would be appropriated as needed to keep the Social Security trust funds at a 100% balance ratio during the transition, protecting benefits for those who do not elect accounts.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers, who would cover the gap left in the trust fund while payroll taxes are diverted into accounts, and electing workers, who trade a guaranteed benefit for an irrevocable market investment that could pay less in a bad market.

drawbacks.text: Electing workers' traditional Social Security benefits are reduced by an offset equal to the annuity their account pays, with a full offset for anyone born in 1979 or later — so opting in means exchanging guaranteed benefits for a 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio that could underperform, and the election cannot be undone.

Because deposits are diverted out of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund while benefit promises are kept, the bill appropriates general Treasury funds to hold the trust funds at a 100% balance ratio, a transition cost financed by taxes or borrowing rather than by payroll revenue.

Under the optional cash distribution, a worker can take part of the account as a lump sum if the remaining amount still funds a minimum annual payment (about $8,590 to $11,610 in 2001 dollars), which opens the door to retirement money being spent early.

The bill directs a study on moving account investment and management from the government board to approved private-sector account managers once balances are large enough, which would shift retirement savings toward fee-charging intermediaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is an unusually protective version of a personal-accounts plan: it guarantees current-law benefits with enforceable certificates, tops off the trust funds with general revenue, requires inflation-indexed annuities, and tilts the deposit rate toward low earners. But the core trade is real — electing workers irrevocably swap a defined government guarantee for market exposure on 60% of their money, the transition is financed by general taxpayers, and the plan builds toward a permanent private asset-management channel whose fees come out of workers' returns. Whether that trade helps a given worker depends entirely on market returns over a career.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Jim DeMint, joined by House Majority Leader Dick Armey, introduced the bill on December 19, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Seven House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained a new benefit: Social Security continued exactly as before, with its guaranteed benefits intact, and the asset-management industry never received the new accounts. Workers who wanted ownership-based accounts gained nothing, and the program's structural financing questions were left unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Social Security as it stood

for.name: Rep. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Ownership and Guarantee Act and sought cosponsors for a personal-accounts restructuring of Social Security.

for.name: Rep. Dick Armey
for.what_they_did: Joined DeMint in introducing the bill as an original sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; after the day-one referral the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican — DeMint, Armey, and 7 cosponsors — no Democrat signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would route workers' retirement savings through professionally managed index portfolios and directs a study, due within five years, on shifting account management from the government board to approved private-sector account managers. That would create a permanent pool of fee-generating accounts, with fees coming out of account owners' returns.

The Executive Director must survey private-sector annuity contracts and use them if their cost is equivalent to in-house annuities, opening a potential market selling the required inflation-indexed, survivor-protected annuities. Retirees need annuity income either way, so the industry's gain does not come at retirees' expense as written.
